items.stem: Leila offered to sell Yusuf a boat for $30 000, promising to keep the offer open until Friday. On Thursday Yusuf heard from Hana, a reliable mutual friend, that Leila had sold the boat to someone else. On Friday morning Yusuf sent an acceptance. Advise Yusuf whether there is a contract. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: an offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance, even if promised to stay open, unless consideration is given (Routledge v Grant); revocation must be communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven); communication can be through a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds). Application: Yusuf gave no consideration for the promise to keep the offer open; Yusuf learned of the sale from Hana, a reliable source, before accepting; so the offer was revoked before acceptance. Conclusion: There is no contract because the offer was effectively revoked before Yusuf accepted.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: identifies revocation of an offer and communication by a third party; accurate statement of the law, e.g. an offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance, even if promised to stay open, unless consideration is given (Routledge v Grant); revocation must be communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven); communication can be through a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds). AO2 Application [1]: applies the rules to the facts, e.g. Yusuf gave no consideration for the promise to keep the offer open; Yusuf learned of the sale from Hana, a reliable source, before accepting; so the offer was revoked before acceptance. Conclusion [1]: there is no contract because the offer was effectively revoked before Yusuf accepted [3]

items.stem: Freya saw a laptop in the window of Mohammed's shop in Bangkok with a label reading "$45". The correct price was ten times higher. When Freya went inside and offered to pay $45, Mohammed refused to sell. Advise Freya whether there is a binding contract with Mohammed. Explain and apply the relevant law, using decided cases to support your advice.
items.answer: Law: goods displayed in a shop are an invitation to treat (Fisher v Bell; Pharmaceutical Society v Boots); the customer makes the offer, which the shopkeeper may accept or reject; a contract needs offer and acceptance. Application: the label on the laptop was an invitation to treat; Freya made the offer to pay $45; Mohammed refused, so there was no acceptance. Conclusion: There is no contract, so Freya cannot insist on buying the laptop for $45.

items.stem: On 1 March Yusuf wrote to Chloe offering to sell 200 laptops for $90 000. Chloe received the letter on 3 March and posted a letter of acceptance on the same day. On 4 March Yusuf emailed Chloe to withdraw the offer. Chloe's letter was lost in the post and never arrived. Advise Chloe whether there is a binding contract. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: acceptance by post takes effect on posting (Adams v Lindsell); this applies even if the letter is lost (Household Fire v Grant); revocation is effective only when received (Byrne v Van Tienhoven); the offeror may exclude the postal rule (Holwell v Hughes). Application: Chloe posted acceptance on 3 March, so the contract was formed then; Yusuf's revocation on 4 March came too late; the fact that the letter was lost in the post and never arrived does not matter. Conclusion: A contract was formed on 3 March when Chloe posted the acceptance, so Yusuf is bound.

items.stem: Kenji owed Felix $10 000. Felix agreed to accept three quarters in full settlement. After Kenji paid three quarters, Felix demanded the remaining balance. Advise Kenji whether Felix can recover the balance. Explain and apply the relevant law, using decided cases to support your advice.
items.answer: Law: part payment is not satisfaction of the whole debt (Pinnel's Case; Foakes v Beer); exceptions: payment earlier, at a different place or with something extra; promissory estoppel may stop Felix going back on the promise if Kenji relied on it and it would be inequitable (High Trees); it is a shield, not a sword. Application: Kenji paid only three quarters with nothing extra; under Foakes v Beer Felix can claim the balance; Kenji may argue promissory estoppel if Kenji relied on Felix's promise. Conclusion: Under the strict rule Felix can recover the balance unless Kenji can rely on promissory estoppel.

items.stem: Jonas Ltd, a hotel chain in Singapore, promised its employee Priya a bonus of $10 000 if Priya achieved record sales. The letter said "This bonus is part of your terms of employment." Priya met the target, but Jonas Ltd refused to pay. Advise Priya whether Priya can enforce the promise. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: commercial agreements are presumed to be binding (Edwards v Skyways); the presumption can be rebutted by clear words such as an honour clause (Rose and Frank v Crompton); promotional gifts in a business context may be binding (Esso v Customs and Excise). Application: the agreement was in a commercial (employment) context; the letter said "This bonus is part of your terms of employment.", so the commercial presumption applies and is not rebutted, so the promise is binding (Edwards v Skyways). Conclusion: The commercial presumption applies and is not rebutted, so the promise is binding (Edwards v Skyways).

items.stem: Evaluate the doctrine of privity of contract.

items.answer: An offer is a definite promise to be bound on specific terms once accepted (Carlill); an invitation to treat is only an invitation to make offers or negotiate, e.g. shop displays (Boots) and most advertisements (Partridge v Crittenden).
items.markingKey: 1 mark offer; 1 mark ITT; 1 mark example/case. [3]

items.stem: Arjun offered to sell Freya a house for $80 000, promising to keep the offer open until Friday. items.answer: There is no contract because the offer was effectively revoked before Freya accepted. Reason: an offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance, even if promised to stay open, unless consideration is given (Routledge v Grant)

items.stem: Aisha saw a designer watch in the window of Tomás's shop in Lisbon with a label reading "$120". The correct price was ten times higher. When Aisha went inside and offered to pay $120, Tomás refused to sell. Advise Aisha whether there is a binding contract with Tomás. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: goods displayed in a shop are an invitation to treat (Fisher v Bell; Pharmaceutical Society v Boots); the customer makes the offer, which the shopkeeper may accept or reject; a contract needs offer and acceptance. Application: the label on the designer watch was an invitation to treat; Aisha made the offer to pay $120; Tomás refused, so there was no acceptance. Conclusion: There is no contract, so Aisha cannot insist on buying the designer watch for $120.

items.stem: Noah put up posters in Riyadh: "$500 reward to anyone who returns my lost parrot." Ethan found the parrot, had not seen the poster and returned it. Advise Ethan whether Ethan is entitled to the reward. Consider all the relevant issues and reach a justified conclusion.
items.answer: Law: an advertisement of a reward can be a unilateral offer to the whole world (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co); acceptance is by performing the act, without notifying the offeror; the person performing must know of the offer to accept it (R v Clarke (1927), Australia). Application: the posters were a unilateral offer; Ethan had not seen the poster. Conclusion: Ethan probably cannot claim because acceptance requires knowledge of the offer.

items.stem: Explain the presumptions relating to intention to create legal relations.
items.answer: Social and domestic agreements are presumed not to be binding (Balfour v Balfour); commercial agreements are presumed to be binding (Edwards v Skyways); both presumptions can be rebutted by evidence, e.g. separation (Merritt) or an honour clause (Rose and Frank).

items.stem: Explain why the law presumes that domestic agreements are not legally binding.
items.answer: Family members do not usually intend to sue each other; enforcing such promises would flood the courts and intrude into family life (Balfour v Balfour).
